For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I'm excited to collaborate on challenges involving Earth science, space exploration, robotics, data analysis, and emerging technologies.
summary:
Crew Health Monitor is a web dashboard that helps astronauts keep an eye on their own health during long missions. Crew members log seven readings: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and blood sugar. Every field has a short step by step guide, so nobody needs medical training to use it.

The dashboard shows each reading as an interactive chart with a normal range, colour coded as Normal, Watch or Alert. A body map explains what each part does and how spaceflight affects it, and the readings are linked to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. It also looks at trends, such as drifting away from their own baseline or several short nights of sleep, and tells the astronaut what to do and when to contact the flight surgeon.

On long missions, help is far away and small changes are easy to miss, so astronauts need to spot problems early. Our prototype runs in the browser with simulated data, and its ranges are illustrative until a flight surgeon reviews them.
details:
What it does and how it works
Crew Health Monitor is a web dashboard that astronauts can use to check on their own health. They enter readings in a short form: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood and how much they exercised. Every field has a step-by-step guide that explains how to take the measurement and why it matters in space. Each reading is compared with a normal range and given a status of Normal, Watch or Alert, and shown on an interactive chart that you can hover for exact times and values. When something is off, the dashboard gives specific advice and says when to contact the flight surgeon. It also looks at trends over time, such as a reading drifting away from the astronaut’s own baseline or several short nights of sleep in a row.

Benefits and intended impact
On a long mission, help is far away and small changes are easy to miss. We want astronauts to catch problems earlier, understand what is happening, and know what to do next without needing medical training. The check in tracker shows what is still missing each day, which helps build a daily habit.

Tools we used
React and Vite for the app, Tailwind CSS for styling, and plain JavaScript for the logic. The charts and the body figure are hand-written SVG, so we didn’t need any chart or 3D library. There is no backend or database. Everything runs in the browser, so it is light and works on a weak connection, and nothing is sent anywhere. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages.

What makes it creative
The glowing body map has hotspots for the brain, chest, heart, abdomen and legs. Hovering one shows what that part does and how spaceflight affects it. Readings are linked to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards, so you can see why a number matters. For the demo, every refresh generates a new simulated mission (a steady one, a stress build-up, or an infection), so people can watch the alerts and trends respond. There is also a light and a dark theme.

What we considered
We wanted the whole dashboard to fit on one screen with no scrolling, because it is a monitoring tool. We used plain language and colour plus text labels, so status never depends on colour alone, and the body hotspots work with a keyboard. We kept the layout responsive for phones and tablets. We were also careful about safety: the normal ranges and advice are illustrative, the data in the demo is simulated, and the app is meant to support the flight surgeon, not replace them. Expert review of the thresholds is the first thing we would do next.
